title: SIP Café
tagline: A mobile-first ordering website for a café in Ramallah.
summary: An ordering website for SIP, a café on Al-Karmel Street in Ramallah: browse the menu, customise a drink, choose how to pay and when you’ll arrive, then follow the order until it’s ready for pickup.
overview: SIP is a café in Ramallah with a simple promise: “Don’t skip, take a SIP”. I designed its website as an ordering experience. Customers open it on their phone, browse drinks and pastries, pick the size, milk and extra shots, and confirm with their name, phone, payment method and the time they’ll arrive. The site was designed for mobile, tablet and desktop; the mobile designs are shown here. Development was done directly with AI using skills, and the café’s admin panel was built the same way. Screens of the build and the admin will be added later.
problem: A small café needs a quick way to take orders before pickup, without phone calls or long message threads, and one clear place for its menu, offers and opening hours.

product: Defined the ordering flow with the client, from menu to pickup
Scoped the pages for mobile, tablet and desktop
Planned the admin panel for the menu and orders
Developed the site and the admin directly with AI, using skills
design: Welcome, cookie consent and opening-hours states
Menu with categories, sub-categories, New and Discount tabs
Product options: size, milk, extra shot, notes and quantity
Cart, checkout with validation, and order status
Empty, loading, error and no-connection states
Social media posts, a pass card and a gift voucher in Canva

process.title: Discover
process.desc: Learned the café’s menu, brand and how customers order today.

process.title: Map the flow
process.desc: Browse, customise, cart, confirm and pick up, in as few steps as possible.

process.title: Design
process.desc: Mobile-first screens in the SIP identity: deep green, the pattern band and script headlines.

process.title: Edge states
process.desc: Closed for now, coming soon, no connection, errors, validation and an empty cart.

process.title: Build with AI

process.desc: Posts, a pass card and a gift voucher in Canva so the brand feels the same everywhere.

challenges.challenge: Customers order on the move, on their phones.
challenges.solution: A mobile-first menu: a greeting, category tabs and sub-category chips, with each product opening as a bottom sheet so the menu stays in view.

challenges.challenge: Drink options get lost in messages.
challenges.solution: One sheet for size, milk, extra shots and notes, with the price updating on the Add to cart button.

challenges.challenge: The café needs to know who is coming, and when.
challenges.solution: A short checkout: name, phone, cash or card on arrival, and an arrival time from 5 to 30 minutes, with clear validation messages.

challenges.challenge: Customers wonder whether their order is ready.
challenges.solution: A confirmation that the order is being prepared, then its status on the cart: Pending, Preparing, Ready for Pickup.

challenges.challenge: The site still has to make sense when the café is closed or offline.
challenges.solution: Dedicated states for Closed for now (with the reopening time), Coming soon, no connection, errors and an empty cart.

learnings: SIP was a chance to discover more design skills on a real client project: designing an ordering flow end to end in one week, keeping a small brand consistent from the website to social media, and working with AI to move from design to a working product faster. It also taught me to design the quiet states, like closed, empty and offline, as carefully as the main flow.

title: WorldClockr
tagline: A clean world clock and time-zone converter.
summary: A mobile app that keeps people in sync with time around the world: local time detected automatically, favourite cities at a glance, and a quick converter between any two cities.
overview: WorldClockr is a modern, intuitive mobile app that helps people stay connected with time across the world. It detects the user’s current location, shows the local time, and lets them add favourite cities for quick access. Users can convert time between two cities and manage their list by reordering or deleting any city.
problem: Many people work or communicate across time zones, but most time apps are cluttered, hard to navigate or offer little customisation. Users end up searching “current time in X” or doing mental maths when scheduling meetings or travel.

design: Research into how people track time zones day to day
Review of gaps in existing time apps
User types, needs and pain points
Wireframes and high-fidelity UI
Testing and iteration

process.title: Empathise
process.desc: Understood user needs, problems and behaviours.

process.title: Define
process.desc: Identified the core challenges and opportunities.

process.title: Ideate
process.desc: Brainstormed and explored creative solutions.

process.title: Design
process.desc: Created wireframes and high-fidelity interfaces.

process.title: Test
process.desc: Validated ideas and improved them from feedback.

challenges.challenge: Checking the time in another city means searching the web every time.
challenges.solution: Local time detected automatically, with favourite cities listed on the home screen and their offset from you (+7h, −2h) and the day (Yesterday, Today, Tomorrow).

challenges.challenge: Scheduling across time zones takes mental maths.
challenges.solution: A two-city converter that shows the time difference in big type, with a swap button to flip the direction.

challenges.challenge: Existing apps are cluttered and hard to navigate.
challenges.solution: One list, two actions in the header (edit and add), and a dark interface with a single pink accent so the time always stands out.

challenges.challenge: Users want their own list, not a fixed one.
challenges.solution: An edit mode to remove or drag cities into any order, and an add-city sheet with suggested cities and search.

learnings: WorldClockr was a chance to explore new design skills on a small, focused product: keeping a utility app simple, making time differences easy to read at a glance, and designing everyday patterns like search, reordering and editing a list. It reminded me that the clearest solution often means removing steps, not adding features.

title: BoxChampy
tagline: A one-page site for a boxing gym.
summary: A bold one-page website for a boxing gym, designed as a personal practice project in visual design, typography and responsive layout.
overview: BoxChampy is a landing page for an imagined boxing gym. I designed it to practise visual design for the web: building a strong first impression with type and photography, guiding the eye down a single page, and carrying one look from desktop to mobile.
problem: How might a boxing gym show its energy in the first few seconds, while still making it easy to see what it offers and how to get in touch?

design: Visual direction and moodboard
Typography and colour
Desktop layout
Mobile version
Final UI

process.title: Explore
process.desc: Collected references from sports and fitness brands to set the mood.

process.title: Type & colour
process.desc: Chose a tall condensed headline type, black and light grey, and one red accent.

process.title: Layout
process.desc: Built the page as three clear parts: hero, story, and a closing call to action.

process.title: Responsive
process.desc: Adapted the same system to a phone screen without losing the bold feel.

challenges.challenge: Making the brand feel strong at first glance.
challenges.solution: A dark, full-width photo with an oversized condensed headline, and red used only on the word that matters: CHAMPION.

challenges.challenge: Moving from the hero into the content without a hard break.
challenges.solution: A diagonal edge between the dark hero and the grey section, with a white card that sits across both.

challenges.challenge: Showing what the gym offers without long text.
challenges.solution: Three quick pillars, Weights, Exercises and Protein, each with a simple line icon and a red label.

challenges.challenge: Keeping the same impact on a small screen.
challenges.solution: On mobile the sections stack, the menu becomes one red button, and the headline, accent and diagonal edge stay the same.

learnings: BoxChampy helped me discover more visual design skills beyond app UI: working with bold type and photography, building one page that guides the eye, and carrying one look from desktop to mobile. Designing it in a single day also showed how much a few strong choices can carry a design: one headline typeface, one accent colour and one shape repeated across the page.
